opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we've been living with very intensely. In a lot of ways the foundations haven't changed. The principles are the same: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability. And the basic practice is the same too. You identify the risks, you measure them, you mitigate them, and then you operate and monitor the system once it's out in the world. That loop still holds.

What's changed is almost everything about how you execute each step. With traditional AI systems, you often had a fairly well-defined task, like a classifier making a specific decision, so you could reason about the inputs and outputs pretty concretely. With generative AI the space of inputs and outputs is essentially open-ended. The same model might be used to write code, summarize a medical document, or chat with someone who's having a hard time. So the risk landscape is much broader, and some of the risks are new: things like ungrounded outputs or hallucinations, jailbreaks and prompt injection, generating harmful content, or questions around copyrighted material.

That breadth really forces you to scale up measurement. You can't just hand-label a test set and call it done. We've had to invest a lot in things like red teaming early to discover what the risks even are, and then turning those findings into systematic, repeatable measurements, often using the models themselves to help generate test cases and evaluate outputs, with humans in the loop to make sure those automated measurements are actually trustworthy.

On the mitigation side, it's very much a layered approach. There's what you do at the model level, but then there's the safety system around it, like content filters and classifiers, then the system message and grounding you put into the application, and finally the user experience: being transparent that people are interacting with AI, designing in ways that help people verify outputs instead of over-relying on them. No single layer is sufficient, but together they get you a lot further.

And the other big shift is pace. Things are moving so quickly, both in capabilities and in how people use these systems, that responsible AI can't be a review at the end. It has to be built into the engineering process and into the tools so that every team, not just a specialized group, can do this work well. A big part of what we've been focused on is taking what we've learned building our own products and turning it into tooling that our customers can use too, because ultimately a lot of the responsibility sits with whoever is building the application for their specific context.

r001.rationale: The response says the foundations and basic practice remain the same, including identifying, measuring, and mitigating risks and monitoring systems.

r002.rationale: It says that “almost everything” about how each step is carried out has changed with generative AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that it's changed in some ways and stayed the same in others. The principles themselves — fairness, reliability and safety, privacy, transparency, accountability — those haven't changed. What's changed dramatically is the practice of actually getting there.

With more traditional machine learning systems, we had a pretty well-developed playbook. You'd have a model that does classification or prediction, you could measure error rates across different groups, you could look at the training data, you could reason about the failure modes fairly concretely. With generative AI, the surface area is just so much larger. A single model can be used for thousands of different tasks, the outputs are open-ended, and the ways it can go wrong are much more varied. So the first big shift is really around measurement — we had to build a whole new set of techniques for evaluating things like groundedness, or whether a model is producing harmful content, or whether it's susceptible to jailbreaks or prompt injection. A lot of that didn't exist two or three years ago.

The second big shift is in the structure of the mitigations. We've landed on this layered approach: you have the safety work that goes into the base model itself, then you have safety systems that sit around the model — content filters, classifiers, that kind of thing — then you have the system message and the application design, and finally the user experience, things like how you communicate the limitations and give people a way to report problems. No single layer solves it, and I think that's an important lesson. Early on there was a lot of hope that you could just get the model right and be done, and that's not how it works in practice.

And the third thing, which I think is actually the most important, is pace. The speed of change in this space is just unlike anything I've worked on before. We're learning new things about these systems constantly, new risks emerge as people use them in ways we didn't anticipate, and so responsible AI can't be a one-time review gate anymore. It has to be an ongoing, iterative process — you measure, you mitigate, you deploy, you monitor, and you keep going around that loop. That's required a real cultural shift inside organizations, not just a technical one.

r001.rationale: The response says the principles themselves have not changed, but says the practice of putting them into action has changed dramatically. It does not state that the overarching task of translating them into practice remains the same.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says the practice of getting to responsible AI has changed dramatically and describes new evaluation methods, layered mitigations, and ongoing iteration.

astra-6.text:
I think generative AI changes both the scale of the challenge and where we need to do the work. The principles still apply—we want systems that are fair, reliable, safe, and transparent, and we need accountability. But translating those principles into something you can measure and improve becomes more complicated when a model can respond to such a wide range of requests.

With a more traditional AI system, you often have a fairly well-defined task. You can ask what failure looks like for that task and build an evaluation around it. With generative AI, you have to consider uses you may not have anticipated, and the same response might be appropriate in one context and harmful in another.

So we need to work at multiple levels: improving the underlying model, putting safeguards into the application, and designing the experience so people understand its limitations and can exercise meaningful control. And we need to keep learning after deployment. Responsible AI becomes an ongoing process of testing, getting feedback, and improving the system, rather than a review you do once before you ship.

r001.rationale: The response says the principles still apply, but does not clearly state that the overarching task of translating them into practice remains the same.

r002.rationale: It describes implementation as changing in scale and focus, becoming more complicated, and requiring work across the model, application, user experience, and post-deployment process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generative AI makes the gap between principles and practice much more visible. Principles like fairness, transparency, and accountability still apply, but we have to translate them into concrete decisions for systems that can do a very broad range of things, including things their developers didn’t anticipate.

With a traditional machine learning system, you often have a fairly well-defined task and can evaluate performance against that task. With generative AI, you need to ask: What is the application? Who will use it? What could go wrong in that context? Evaluating the underlying model is important, but it doesn’t tell you everything about the system people will actually experience.

So responsible AI becomes a continuous process. You test for potential harms, bring in people with different perspectives to challenge the system, build mitigations, and then monitor how those mitigations work in practice. And you need ways to learn from feedback and update the system as new issues emerge.

The other change is that many more people are now building AI applications. We need to make responsible development tools and guidance accessible to those developers, so putting the principles into practice becomes part of building the product from the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response says responsible AI principles still apply, but it does not state that the overarching task of translating them into practice remains the same.

r002.rationale: The response describes changes to implementation, including evaluating applications in context, treating responsibility as continuous, and making tools and guidance accessible to more developers.
